headline: MACC says a CEO took bribes to release payment, not to win the contract
context: On 13 April 2026, MACC detained the chief executive of a federal statutory body over an alleged bribe tied to a RM7 million squash-court project. The main MACC reports did not name the body. The suspect was remanded for five days; no charge has been reported.

cards.big: MACC's allegation was not that a chief rigged a contract. It was that he charged to release payment on one already running.
cards.sub: The squash-court project was worth RM7 million. The suspect, a man in his 40s, was held at a Bukit Jalil shopping complex on 13 April 2026.

cards.big: The alleged ask was RM1 million to approve the contractor's payment claims; about RM600,000 is said to have changed hands.
cards.sub: MACC's account: RM500,000 before Hari Raya as an advance, then RM100,000 in cash at the arrest. No report says the full RM1 million was paid.

cards.big: He was remanded five days to assist the probe. No charge has been reported.
cards.sub: Magistrate Ezrene Zakaria issued the order in Putrajaya on 14 April 2026, running to 18 April. A remand allows detention for investigation; it is not a finding of guilt.

cards.big: An alleged RM1 million skims 14% off a RM7 million job, charged simply to sign what the contractor had already earned.
cards.sub: MACC has said public-procurement complaints often centre on approving claims, including for work not properly done, rather than on the original award.

cards.big: Watchdogs guard the tender. The bigger leak may sit one step later, at the desk that signs off the contractor's claims.
Whether charges follow or not, the lesson is the payment desk: scrutiny that stops at the award misses where the cash actually moves.

sources: Bernama 14 Apr 2026; The Star 14 Apr 2026; Malay Mail 14 Apr 2026; FMT 14 Apr 2026; The Edge 14 Apr 2026; The Vibes 14 Apr 2026; The Sun/Bernama 8 Aug 2024; CPC Act 593 s.28/s.117
